prompt.context: Your client is Barlly Inc., a cosmetic company based in the US. Barlly has business both in the US and globally. Currently, the client is facing a high level of inventory in the US and is hiring McKinsey to help solve the problem. The client has had the inventory problem for quite a while, so it is a structural problem rather than a one-off problem. The client sources raw materials from all over the world. The client has one manufacturing site near Chicago and 4 distribution centers across the US. The client maintains its inventory at DCs — when products are manufactured, they are directly sent to DCs. The client sells to all kinds of retailers across the US. Sales is seasonal with peaks before major holidays.
prompt.question: How can the client reduce its inventory in the short-term? What are possible reasons for the high inventory level and how can the client improve in the long term?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's forecast accuracy?
clarifying_info.a: The client has an average forecast error of +/- 25%.

clarifying_info.q: Are there constraints on minimum order quantities from suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: Some raw materials have very high minimum order quantities (MOQ), and large purchases for such materials build up inventory.

clarifying_info.q: How often does the client replenish DCs from the manufacturing site?
clarifying_info.a: The replenishment cycle is currently once a week.

clarifying_info.q: How is the procurement department evaluated?
clarifying_info.a: Procurement is only evaluated by service level, so they tend to build up inventory to ensure material availability.

clarifying_info.q: Are there constraints on batch size in manufacturing?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there is a mechanical constraint that a large quantity has to be made in a single run (large batch size).

clarifying_info.q: Do suppliers reliably meet delivery schedules?
clarifying_info.a: Some suppliers often miss delivery times and production windows, causing delays and leaving other raw materials sitting in inventory waiting for missing ingredients.

framework: Map the end-to-end supply chain / value chain: Forecast → Procurement → Manufacturing → Distribution → Sales
Short-term: reduce production and increase sales to drain existing inventory
Long-term: analyze each step of the value chain for root causes of inventory buildup
Prioritize initiatives by impact and ease of implementation
Address organizational incentives and employee mindset alongside process fixes

questions.prompt: How can the client reduce inventory in the short term?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two primary levers — cut supply (reduce production) and boost demand/offload stock. Strong answers cover both sides and offer multiple tactics for each.

questions.prompt: Walk through the value chain and identify the root causes of high inventory at each stage. Start with Forecasting.
questions.guidance: Forecast error of +/-25% means the client is frequently over-ordering. Because lead times for some raw materials are long, the client can't wait for the most accurate forecast. Candidate should suggest negotiating with suppliers to shorten lead times, or pre-building strategic stock for long-lead materials so the final production order can use the latest, more accurate forecast.

questions.prompt: What procurement-level issues could be driving high inventory?
questions.guidance: Three key issues: (1) High MOQ from some suppliers forces bulk purchases — fix by negotiating lower MOQs. (2) Supplier delivery non-compliance delays production and strands other materials — fix by improving supplier compliance or switching suppliers. (3) Procurement is evaluated solely on service level, creating an incentive to over-stock — fix by adding inventory level to performance metrics.

questions.prompt: What manufacturing-level issues could be driving high inventory?
questions.guidance: Large minimum batch sizes mean production runs generate more finished goods than needed in the short term. Fix: invest in equipment and R&D to reduce minimum batch size.

questions.prompt: What distribution-level issues could be driving high inventory?
questions.guidance: Two issues: (1) Safety stock is held at every DC independently. Centralizing inventory at the manufacturing site (or one central DC) reduces total required safety stock by the square root of the number of DCs — with 4 DCs, centralization roughly halves total safety stock. (2) Weekly replenishment cycle drives large cycle stocks. Increasing replenishment frequency reduces average cycle stock.

math.setup: If safety stock is maintained at each of 4 DCs independently, total safety stock = 4 × S. Centralizing reduces it by a factor of sqrt(4) = 2, so total safety stock = 4S / 2 = 2S — a 50% reduction.
steps: Centralized safety stock = original total / 2 → roughly 50% reduction
math.answer: Centralizing inventory at one location reduces total safety stock by approximately 50%.

questions.prompt: Are there any system-wide or cultural issues driving excess inventory?
questions.guidance: The client places high emphasis on service level across the entire value chain. As a result, every step independently adds safety stock to protect its own service level. These buffers stack up. Fix: maintain safety stock only at the finished-goods level and eliminate intermediate safety stocks. Additionally, build an inventory-management mindset among employees and provide proper tools.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible reasons for the client's high inventory level across the value chain?

categories.name: Forecasting
ideas: High forecast error (+/- 25%) leads to over-ordering
Long raw material lead times prevent using latest forecast
Seasonal demand not adequately factored into forecasts

categories.name: Procurement
ideas: High minimum order quantities (MOQ) force bulk purchases
Supplier delivery non-compliance strands partially-assembled inventory
Procurement team incentivized only on service level, not inventory efficiency

categories.name: Manufacturing
ideas: Large minimum batch sizes produce more than needed
Single manufacturing site limits production flexibility

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Safety stock duplicated across 4 DCs inflates total inventory
Weekly replenishment cycle creates large cycle stocks
No centralized inventory visibility across DCs

categories.name: System / Culture
ideas: Every supply chain step independently buffers for service level, causing stacking safety stocks
Lack of inventory management mindset among employees
No proper inventory management tools or KPIs below the service-level metric

recommendation: Short-term: Immediately reduce production to stop adding to excess inventory, and accelerate inventory liquidation through price reductions, volume discounts, outlet channels, marketing promotions, or export to overseas markets.

Long-term: Systematically fix each link in the supply chain — negotiate shorter lead times and lower MOQs with suppliers, improve supplier compliance, reduce manufacturing batch sizes, centralize safety stock at the finished-goods level, and increase DC replenishment frequency.
risks: Reducing production may strain the manufacturing facility or create restart costs when demand returns.
Aggressive discounting or dumping inventory overseas may dilute brand equity.
Centralizing inventory increases exposure to supply disruption at a single node.
Supply chain fixes require supplier negotiations that may take time and have uncertain outcomes.
next_steps: Add inventory level metrics to procurement department's performance evaluation.
Build an inventory management capability (tools + training) across the supply chain.
Negotiate lead times and MOQs with top raw material suppliers.
Pilot centralized inventory model and higher replenishment frequency at one DC before full rollout.
Invest in improved demand forecasting (data, process, and systems).
